This section describes the architectures that lead from hand-designed pipelines to learned features: Rowley’s face detector, LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet with its inception modules, ResNet, DenseNet, and the Vision Transformer. For each network, we look at its layer structure, the problem its design solved, its size, and its results on the benchmark of its time.

In 1998, Henry Rowley, Shumeet Baluja, and Takeo Kanade at Carnegie Mellon University published a neural face detector that worked on cluttered photos. Its design keeps the network small and moves most of the work into fixed processing steps around it.
shows the version that also finds rotated faces.

children.alt: Rowley’s rotation-invariant face detector: image pyramid, router network, preprocessing, and detection network.

children.value: Rowley’s rotation-invariant face detector: image pyramid, router network, preprocessing, and detection network.

The detector examines windows of 20 by 20 pixels. To find faces larger than the window, it builds an image pyramid: it reduces the image repeatedly by a factor of 1.2 and applies the network at every pixel position of every level. Each window passes two preprocessing steps. First, a linear brightness function fitted to an oval face region is subtracted to compensate for uneven lighting. Second, histogram equalization stretches the contrast.

The detection network receives the 400 preprocessed pixel values, but its hidden units do not see the whole window. Four hidden units look at 10 by 10 subregions, 16 at 5 by 5 subregions, and 6 at overlapping horizontal stripes of 20 by 5 pixels. The stripes can detect a pair of eyes or a mouth, and the square fields can detect single eyes, the nose, or the corners of the mouth. The final systems replicate these hidden units two or three times. A single output unit makes the decision: it is trained to produce
for anything else. The local fields resemble the receptive fields of a convolutional layer, but they are fixed by hand, and their weights are not shared across positions.

Face examples are easy to collect: the authors gathered about 1050 of them from face databases. Examples of nonfaces are harder, because almost any image region is a nonface. A bootstrap procedure solves this. The network is trained, applied to 120 scenery images that contain no faces, and every false detection is added to the training set as a negative example; then the network is trained again. A typical run selected about 8000 nonface windows out of 146 million available subimages. At detection time, overlapping detections are merged, and several networks vote. The upright detector found 90.5% of the faces in a test set of 130 complex images.

Every step except the final decision was designed by hand: the window size, the lighting correction, the histogram equalization, the derotation, and the sliding-window search. This made the method hard to reuse. A detector for cats or dogs would need its own preprocessing, its own receptive fields, and its own training set. Neural classifiers of this generation were optimized for one task and did not adapt to a new one without human work.

Yann LeCun and colleagues at AT&T Bell Labs developed LeNet in several versions between 1989 and 1998, first to read zip codes and later bank checks. LeNet-5, described in full by LeCun and colleagues in 1998, is the version usually meant. Its test bed was the MNIST database with 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of handwritten digits. The digits come from NIST collections written by Census Bureau employees and high school students on forms like the one in

. Each digit was scaled to fit into a 20 by 20 pixel box while keeping its aspect ratio, which introduced gray levels through anti-aliasing, and then placed into a 28 by 28 image with its center of mass in the center.

Counting the layers of LeNet-5 gives 60,000 trainable parameters: 156 in C1, 12 in S2, 1,516 in C3, 32 in S4, 48,120 in the layer with 120 units, and 10,164 in the layer with 84 units. Four fifths of them sit in the first dense layer, which connects all 400 values of S4 to 120 units. The original output layer, which compares the 84 values with hand-chosen prototypes of the ten digits, is not counted. The fully connected variant in the figure has 61,706 parameters.

LeNet-5 reached a test error of 0.95% on MNIST, about 99% accuracy, and 0.8% when the training set was enlarged with distorted copies of the digits. The network learned its features from the pixels; apart from the size normalization of the digits, nobody designed a feature. Yet a support vector machine reached a comparable 0.8% in the same comparison, and convolutional networks remained a specialist tool for more than a decade. Today, ensembles of convolutional networks with data augmentation reach error rates below 0.1% on MNIST. The
trains a small convolutional network in the browser and visualizes the network while it learns.

AlexNet, by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) of 2012. The challenge asks for one of 1000 classes per image, a large step from the ten classes of digit recognition, and provides about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 150,000 test images. children.value: Several design choices made the training of such a network possible. The ReLU activation replaced the saturating tanh: a four-layer network with ReLUs reached a training error of 25% on CIFAR-10 six times faster than the same network with tanh units. A single GTX 580 GPU with 3 GB of memory limited the size of the network, so the authors split it across two GPUs. The second, fourth, and fifth convolutions connect only to the feature maps on the same GPU, and training took five to six days. Overlapping pooling, with windows of 3 and stride 2, reduced the top-1 and top-5 error rates by 0.4% and 0.3% compared with non-overlapping pooling. Local response normalization follows the first two convolutions. Against overfitting, the authors used data augmentation, with random

children.html: 224×224224 \times 224224×224

children.value: crops, horizontal reflections, and color changes along the principal components of the RGB values, and dropout in the first two dense layers. Without dropout, the network overfitted substantially.

A single AlexNet reached a top-5 error of 18.2% on the validation data, and the average of five networks 16.4%. The winning entry averaged seven networks, two of which had been pretrained on the full ImageNet release of fall 2011 with 15 million images in 22,000 categories, and reached a top-5 test error of 15.3%. The second-best entry, which classified Fisher vectors of hand-crafted features, reached 26.2%.

VGG placed second in the classification task of ILSVRC 2014, with a top-5 test error of 7.3% for an ensemble of seven networks, and first in localization. After the competition, an ensemble of two networks reached 6.8%, and the best single network 7.0%. The simple, uniform design made VGG a popular feature extractor for years.

GoogLeNet, by Christian Szegedy and colleagues at Google, won the classification task of ILSVRC 2014. Its name is a homage to LeNet. The task had the same format as in 2012: 1000 classes, about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 100,000 test images. The challenge with 200 object classes is the separate detection task. GoogLeNet was designed for efficiency, with a budget of 1.5 billion multiply-adds per image at inference.

During training, their losses are added to the total loss with a weight of 0.3, to strengthen the gradient signal that reaches the lower layers and to regularize the network. At inference, they are discarded. Later networks with batch normalization and residual connections train without them. An ensemble of seven GoogLeNets, each evaluated on 144 crops per image, reached a top-5 error of 6.67%; a single network on a single crop reached 10.07%.

Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun at Microsoft Research addressed a puzzle. On CIFAR-10, a plain network with 56 layers had a higher training error, and thus a higher test error, than a network with 20 layers. This degradation is not overfitting, since the training error itself gets worse. A deeper network could in principle copy the shallower one and turn its extra layers into the identity, but the training procedure does not find this solution.

Despite its 152 layers, it needs 11.3 billion multiply-adds per image, fewer than VGG-16 with 15.3 billion and VGG-19 with 19.6 billion. Counting its layers gives 60.2 million parameters; ResNet-50 has 25.6 million.

A single ResNet-152 reached a top-5 validation error of 4.49%, and an ensemble a top-5 test error of 3.57%, which won the classification task of ILSVRC 2015. ResNets also won ImageNet detection and localization and the COCO detection and segmentation tasks of that year. On CIFAR-10, the authors even trained a network with 1202 layers without optimization difficulty. Its test error of 7.93% was worse than the 6.43% of a 110-layer network, which the authors attribute to overfitting: 19.4 million parameters are too many for this small dataset.

children.value: A convolution builds two assumptions about images into the network: nearby pixels belong together, and a pattern means the same wherever it appears. The Vision Transformer has far less of this image-specific bias. Apart from cutting the image into patches, it must learn spatial relations from data. Trained on ImageNet alone, with 1.3 million images, ViT models end a few percentage points below ResNets of comparable size. Pretrained on ImageNet-21k with 14 million images, or on Google’s internal JFT-300M with 303 million images, they match or beat the best convolutional networks: ViT-H/14 pretrained on JFT-300M reaches 88.55% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, ViT-L/16 87.76%, and ViT-L/16 pretrained on ImageNet-21k 85.30%.
